input:
This assessment covers the energy use of a dairy plant and recommends one measure: a heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant. The case for the measure rests on electricity, which is the plant's largest metered load. The steam figures available to the assessment are seasonal and cannot support an annual claim, and the recommendation is written on that basis.

## Current use

Electricity use at the plant comes to a total of 2264 MWh per year, and it is worth noting that refrigeration accounts for the largest share of that total. The remaining load is spread across the process drives, the filling and packing lines, compressed air, lighting and the various services that support production. The pattern of use follows the pattern of production quite closely: intake, separation and pasteurisation set the daytime load, the cold stores hold a load through the night, and cleaning at the end of each production run adds a further block of demand on both electricity and steam. Because the load is production-led, it rises and falls with throughput rather than with the weather alone, and it is the refrigeration plant that carries the consequences first, since every litre of milk that arrives warm must be cooled and then held cold until it leaves the site. No single item of process equipment rivals the refrigeration load, and measures that are aimed at the smaller loads cannot move the annual total by very much. The assessment therefore concentrates on refrigeration: it is the largest load, it runs for the most hours, and it rejects heat that the plant currently pays to throw away while paying again to raise hot water and steam elsewhere on the site.

## Refrigeration

The refrigeration plant serves the cold stores, the chilled-water circuit and the process cooling duties, and it runs whenever production or storage requires it, which in practice means most of the year. Its compressors reject heat at the condensers, and that heat is at present simply discharged to atmosphere. The quantity of heat involved is large, because it covers both the heat that is removed from the product and the work done by the compressors in removing it. A dairy plant, meanwhile, has a standing demand for warm water: washing down, cleaning in place and general services all draw hot water through the day, and the first stage of that heating is currently done with steam raised in the boiler house. Heat recovered from the refrigeration condensers can do that first stage instead, lifting cold water part of the way so that the boiler only has to supply the remaining rise. The retrofit examined in this assessment is of exactly that kind: a heat-recovery stage on the refrigeration plant, piped into the hot-water system, with the existing steam heating retained for the final lift and for duties that the recovered heat cannot reach. The match between the two sides is good in principle, because the hours when refrigeration rejects the most heat are broadly the hours when production is running and hot water is being drawn, although the match is not exact and a buffer volume is needed to carry recovered heat across the gaps. The heat that is available at the condensers is low-grade heat: warm, rather than hot. It cannot displace steam in the pasteuriser or in any duty that needs a high temperature, and the retrofit does not attempt those duties. Its field is the preheating field, where water enters cold and any heat put into it at that stage is heat that the boiler does not have to supply later. Working in that field also keeps the refrigeration plant itself undisturbed in its duty: the compressors condense as before, and the recovery stage takes heat that was previously rejected, so the cooling performance the plant depends on is not traded against the saving. Control of the recovered stream has to follow the hot-water demand rather than the refrigeration load, diverting heat to the air when the water side cannot take it, so that a failure or a quiet period on the water side never backs up into the cooling side.

## Steam

Steam is raised in the boiler house and is used for pasteurisation, for cleaning and for space heating in the production areas. The steam figures that are available to this assessment come from one winter month, and they are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation that follows. A winter month will tend to overstate the steam demand of the year as a whole: space heating is at its peak, incoming milk and water are at their coldest, and the boiler runs under conditions that the summer months do not reproduce. The figures are still usable for the shape of the steam load, for the split between process and heating duties, and for the state of the distribution system, where condensate return and insulation can be judged from inspection in any month. They are not, however, usable as the basis of an annual steam saving, and no annual figure for steam is carried into the recommendation. A full year of steam metering, read alongside production, is needed before any steam-side measure can be costed on the same footing as the refrigeration measure. That gap does not weaken the electricity case, which rests on metered electricity data, but it does mean that the assessment is complete on one side of the plant's energy use and provisional on the other.

## Recommendation

The recommendation is to proceed with the heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant. The retrofit is projected to save 13% of electricity use, a derived saving of 294 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $176k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $35318, and the derived simple payback is 5 years. The saving is a projection based on the measured refrigeration load and the hot-water demand it would displace, rather than a measured result, and it should be verified after installation by metering the recovered heat and the boiler fuel it replaces. The steam side of the plant is excluded from this case: the steam figures behind the assessment are from one winter month and are seasonal, so no steam saving is claimed and no steam measure is recommended until a full year of steam data exists. On the electricity figures alone, the retrofit pays back well inside the life of the equipment it modifies, and it also reduces the load on the boiler house as a side effect of displacing the first stage of water heating. The plant should therefore treat the decision as an electricity decision, taken on metered data, with the steam review to follow once the metering year is complete. Installation should be planned into a scheduled stop, so that the refrigeration plant is opened once and the hot-water alterations are made in the same window; the buffer volume and the diverting control described in the refrigeration section are part of the measure, not options on it, since without them the recovered heat cannot follow the demand. After installation, the recovered heat and the boiler fuel should be metered together for a full production cycle, and the measured saving compared with the projection before any further heat-recovery stage is considered.
